# SIDEREAL OBSERVATIONS

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
you encounter a crowd of stars. Furthermore, and what is more wonderful, the stars which have been called **NEBULAE** <gloss>clouds</gloss> by every astronomer up to this day are in fact groups of stars sown together in a marvelous way. From the mingling of their rays, that whiteness arises which has been believed until now to be a denser part of the heavens, capable of reflecting the rays of the stars or the Sun. This happens because each individual star escapes the keenness of our sight, either because of its smallness or its very great distance from us. We have observed several of these, and we wished to add the star charts <note>original: "Asterismos"</note> of two of them.

In the first, you have the **NEBULA** called the Head of Orion, in which we have counted twenty-one stars.

The second contains the **NEBULA** named **PRAESEPE** <gloss>the Manger</gloss>, which is not just one star, but a mass of more than forty small stars. We have noted thirty-six stars, besides the **Aselli** <gloss>the Little Asses</gloss>, arranged in the order that follows.

<note>A telescopic star chart depicts the **ORION NEBULA** </note><note>original: "Nebulosa Orionis"</note>, showing twenty-one individual stars. This scientific diagram represents one of the first telescopic proofs that nebulae are composed of stars rather than being celestial clouds.

<column-break/>

<note>A telescopic star chart depicts the **PRAESEPE NEBULA** </note><note>original: "Nebulosa Praesepe"</note>, also known as the Beehive Cluster, showing over thirty-six stars including the **Aselli** <gloss>the Little Asses</gloss>. This scientific illustration demonstrates the resolution of a nebula into a star cluster through the use of the early telescope.

->THE PRAESEPE NEBULA.<-

->THE ORION NEBULA.<-

<summary>Galileo reveals that what astronomers previously called nebulae are actually clusters of stars invisible to the naked eye. He provides specific star counts and telescopic diagrams for the Orion nebula and the Praesepe cluster to prove his discovery.</summary>
<keywords>Orion, Praesepe, nebulae, star clusters, astronomy, Galileo Galilei, telescope, Aselli</keywords>
